title: How do you answer "What is your biggest achievement?" in a consulting interview?
description: How to answer impact and achievement questions in consulting interviews, with weak and strong example answers that make your role and results clear.
hook: Interviewers want to see that you make things happen, and that you can explain your role clearly. The common mistake is choosing something impressive where your personal part is unclear.
body:
The question

What is the achievement you are most proud of?

A weak answer

I was part of the team that launched our company's new app, which now has over a million users.

Why it falls short: Impressive, but the speaker's role is invisible. The interviewer will ask "what did you do?" and the story starts again.

A strong answer

I noticed that 40% of people who started our online sign-up gave up at the identity check. Nobody owned the problem, so I pulled the data, interviewed ten people who had dropped out, and found the photo upload failed on older phones. I worked with an engineer to add a manual alternative and rewrote the instructions. Completion rose from 60% to 78% within a month, about 2,000 extra customers a month. I'm proud of it because I spotted it, nobody asked me to, and I saw it through.

Why it works: The personal role is unmistakable, the result is quantified, and it shows initiative as well as impact.

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "What is the achievement you are most proud of?" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.

Separate your contribution from the team's headline result

A large result is not compelling if your own role remains invisible. Saying "Our app reached a million customers" invites the obvious question: what exactly did you do to make that happen? Describe your starting point, the decision you owned, your evidence and the measured effect.

Consider a hypothetical marketing analytics example. An organisation receives 200,000 qualified leads per quarter and converts 4% into paying customers, or 8,000 customers. The candidate identifies that one lead segment has unusually poor follow-up and proposes routing those leads to a specialist team. A pilot indicates conversion could improve to 5%. At the same lead volume, that would be 10,000 customers, 2,000 more per quarter, if the improvement held across the full base. Do not claim that projected 2,000 as a realised outcome until rollout data supports it.

In an interview, state what you personally built, persuaded others to change or delivered. Give the baseline and actual result over a defined period. If several teams contributed, acknowledge them explicitly and explain where your work fitted. An honest measured improvement is stronger than an inflated company-wide number.

Finish with a trade-off or learning: perhaps the specialist team handled fewer total leads, or the pilot revealed a need for better lead qualification. Impact is not just a KPI increase; it is an improvement linked to an objective, with enough evidence to believe the cause.
